packages.script: Company property? Our office manager posted a memo: the fridge and the counter are company property, and personal items would be removed and binned. Fine. The coffee maker was mine. The kettle belonged to a woman in accounts. The mugs, toaster, the tin of decent teabags, and the fruit bowl somebody restocked out of her own pocket were all personal property—carried out to our cars in a laundry bag by 5 p.m., exactly as instructed. Compliance achieved. By day three, forty people were walking to the petrol station for coffee while the manager drank hot water from a paper cup. She emailed a second memo asking us to please bring our things back. We returned one thing: an order form. The company has bought the coffee ever since. Who really owned that break-room problem?
packages.editor_note: Punched up to a two-word question hook, tightened the collective compliance escalation, added one dry aside, and landed on the break-room ownership reversal while preserving every fact, number, shot phrase, and query.

packages.script: Scam the scammer? The caller said my bank account had been compromised and the only way to protect my savings was to buy gift cards. A sensible person hangs up. I didn't. I said I was seventy-one and frightened and needed help finding the shop, so he stayed on the line for two hours. He coached me through the aisle of a hardware store while I read codes from eleven cards. Every code I read was wrong by one digit, and each failure made him demand another card. My other phone connected to the card issuer's fraud team, and I passed them the real numbers at the register as I bought them. They froze all eleven and flagged the account redeeming them. He rang back nine times. His last voicemail threatened to report me. Who reported the gift-card scammer first?
packages.editor_note: Punched up to a three-word question hook, compressed the two-phone counter-scam, and landed on the reporting reversal without levity because the story involves a crime victim; every fact, number, shot phrase, and query is preserved.

authored_explainer.title: Cereal Production Is 1.5x Higher Than In 1972
authored_explainer.hook: The 1970s warned the world would run out of food. The numbers refused to cooperate.
says: In 1985, progression to secondary school (%) was 77.8. By 2017, it reached 91.3 — 1.2 times higher.
In 1972, cereal production was 1083.7 million metric tons. By 2024, it reached 1644.1 million metric tons — 1.5 times higher.
China leads at 5.2 million square kilometers of farmland, then the United States at 4.2 million, Australia at 3.6 million, Brazil at 2.4 million, and Russia at 2.2 million.
authored_explainer.closing: The famine everyone predicted never arrived. School advanced, grain climbed, and the forecast was left waiting.
authored_explainer.question: Which shift changed the story most — school, grain, or land?

authored_explainer.title: Combustible Renewables And Waste Is 3.0x Higher Than In 1990
authored_explainer.hook: Since 1990, one energy source tripled. It wasn't solar or wind.
says: In 1990, combustible renewables and waste was 10.2 % of total energy. By 2024, it reached 30.1 % of total energy — 3.0 times higher.
In 1998, access to electricity was 73.2 % of population. By 2024, it reached 91.9 % of population — 1.3 times higher.
In 1972, methane (ch4) emissions from waste was 903.8 Mt CO2e. By 2024, it reached 1,652 Mt CO2e — 1.8 times higher.
authored_explainer.closing: The world's overlooked energy story is built from what people once treated as waste.
authored_explainer.question: Which shift stands out most — fuel, power, or waste?

authored_explainer.title: Population Growth Fell 54% Since 1972
authored_explainer.hook: Population growth was supposed to keep accelerating forever. Instead, the curve nearly stopped.
says: In 1972, rural population was 63.1 % of total population. By 2025, it was 42.2 % of total population — down to 67 percent of that.
In 1972, population in the largest city was 18.2 % of urban population. By 2025, it was 16.2 % of urban population — barely moved.
In 1972, population growth was 2 annual %. By 2025, it was 0.91 annual % — down to 46 percent of that.
authored_explainer.closing: The planet is still growing. What nearly vanished is the acceleration everyone assumed would continue.
authored_explainer.question: Which change surprised you most — rural, city, or growth?
